opus-5.5.text:
I think there's some truth to it, but it's also a bit of a misleading saying, at least for research. I've heard the phrase that "ideas are cheap," and I've also heard people respond, "if ideas are so cheap, how come no one's having any?" And I think that response captures something real.

In research, the bottleneck has shifted over time. For a while, maybe five or so years, the field was in an age of scaling. There was one big idea, which was that if you take a neural network and make it bigger and train it on more data, it gets better. That idea was so powerful, and so clearly correct, that execution really did become everything. If you knew the recipe, the main question was how well you could build the infrastructure, gather the compute, and run the thing without making mistakes. So in that regime, yes, ideas were cheap, because everyone had the same idea.

But I think we're moving back into a period where that's no longer sufficient. Scaling is still important, but just doing more of the same thing doesn't give you the qualitative leaps it once did. And so now we're in a situation where there are many more companies than there are ideas. Everyone is doing roughly similar things, and the differentiation is going to come from genuinely new understanding: how to make these systems generalize better, how to make them learn more efficiently, more like the way people learn.

And when you're in that kind of situation, ideas are not cheap. Good ideas are very rare. What's maybe true is that bad ideas are cheap, or that ideas that haven't been tested are cheap. You still need excellent execution to find out whether an idea is right. But execution without the right idea just gets you a well-engineered version of what everyone else already has.

One more thing I'd say is that you often don't need as much compute as people think to test whether an idea is promising. Historically, a lot of the important breakthroughs were demonstrated on fairly modest amounts of compute. So the idea part, the research taste part, deciding what's actually worth trying, I think that's becoming the scarce resource again.

r001.rationale: The response says good ideas are very rare and that research taste is becoming a scarce resource again.

r002.rationale: It mentions historical breakthroughs using modest compute, but does not identify the 1990s or say limited compute prevented convincing demonstrations.

r003.rationale: It says promising ideas often need less compute than people think, but does not clearly compare that need with compute already available today.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that saying is mostly true in the world it came from, and mostly wrong in research, and it's worth being precise about why.

In a startup, the idea is usually something many people have had. The thing that's scarce is the willingness to grind for five years, hire well, not die. So "execution is everything" is a reasonable heuristic there.

In research, I'd say it differently. The ideas that matter are not cheap at all. They're very rare. But they look cheap in retrospect, because once you have them they seem obvious. "Just scale it up." "Just predict the next token." Anyone can say those sentences. Very few people believed them before the evidence arrived, and even fewer believed them enough to bet years of their life on it. So what's actually scarce is not the sentence but the conviction behind the sentence, the taste that tells you which of the hundred plausible-sounding ideas is the one that's actually going to work.

And then there's a subtlety, which is that in research, the idea and the execution are not separable the way the saying implies. When you try to execute, the idea changes. You discover that the thing you thought was the point was not the point, and some detail you considered boring turns out to be the whole game. The people who do great research are the people who stay in contact with the idea while executing, who keep asking "what is this really telling me," rather than just turning the crank.

So if I had to compress it: in research, taste is everything, and execution is how you find out whether you have any.

r001.rationale: The response says that important research ideas are very rare and that taste identifies which ideas may work, presenting ideas as a scarce resource in research.

r002.rationale: It does not mention 1990s compute limits or researchers being unable to demonstrate ideas convincingly.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that demonstrating a new research idea can be done with roughly the compute available today.

astra-6.text:
I think in research, ideas and execution are much harder to separate. An idea might be, “If we do this particular experiment, we’ll learn something important.” But choosing that experiment is a huge part of the work. You could execute a thousand other experiments perfectly and learn very little.

There is a version of the saying that is true: having a vague idea is not enough. You need to make it precise, get it to work, and understand what the results mean. Often, doing that requires more ideas. So I would say that good execution in research contains a lot of good ideas. The distinction is not as clean as the saying suggests.

r001.rationale: The response says research execution involves choosing good experiments and ideas, but does not identify a scarcity of ideas as a bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not mention 1990s compute limits or researchers being unable to demonstrate promising ideas convincingly.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about how much compute demonstrating a new idea requires or what compute is available today.

sol-6.1.text:
I think in research, the distinction between ideas and execution is not so clear. An idea can be very easy to state after you know that it works. But before you know that it works, it’s one of a thousand possibilities. Why should you pursue this one? Why should you keep pursuing it when the first experiment doesn’t work?

So having the right idea—and having the conviction to really test it—is a very big part of research. Execution matters enormously, of course. You need to do the experiments carefully, and you need to notice what they’re telling you. But if you execute perfectly on something that isn’t going to work, you won’t get very far.

I would say the scarce thing is good judgment. Choosing what to try, figuring out why it failed, deciding whether to persist or move on. That’s hard to separate into an ideas part and an execution part.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls good judgment scarce and says choosing ideas matters, but does not identify scarcity of ideas themselves as a research bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about compute limits in the 1990s or their effect on demonstrating ideas.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about how much compute demonstrating a new idea requires today.
